title: Aeroplanes and helicopters
description: How a wing holds an aeroplane up, why it stalls, how much runway it needs and how far it flies — and how a helicopter rotor hovers, beats torque and lands without an engine. Ends with sizing an aeroplane using the Breguet equation.

aero-01-sustentacao.title: How the wing generates lift
aero-01-sustentacao.theory:
# Pushing the air down

A wing is tilted and curved in a way that **deflects the air downwards**. By **Newton's 3rd law**, if the wing pushes the air down, the air pushes the wing **up**. Seen another way (Bernoulli), the air moves faster over the top of the wing and the **pressure on top is lower** than underneath. The two explanations describe the same phenomenon.

## The lift formula

```
L = ½ · ρ · v² · S · CL
```

- `L` = lift (N)
- `ρ` = air density (1.225 kg/m³ at sea level)
- `v` = speed relative to the air (m/s)
- `S` = wing area (m²)
- `CL` = lift coefficient: depends on the **angle of attack** and the wing profile

Note the **v²**: double the speed gives **four times** the lift.

## Level flight

To fly level, the lift must be **equal to the weight** (L = W = m·g). If L > W the aeroplane climbs; if L < W, it descends. The pilot adjusts the angle of attack (pulling or pushing the stick) according to the speed.

In the simulator, the aeroplane (Cessna 172 style: 1100 kg, 16 m² wing) is at 150 km/h. The arrows show lift (green) and weight (red).
aero-01-sustentacao.task: Make the aeroplane fly **level**: lift between **100% and 110% of the weight**, without stalling.
hints: Increase the angle of attack gradually and watch the green arrow.
At 150 km/h, an angle of attack of 5.5° makes the lift slightly above the weight.
goals: Lift between 100% and 110% of the weight

questions.prompt: A **10 m²** wing flies at **50 m/s** with CL = **0.5** (ρ = 1.2 kg/m³). What is the lift?
If the speed **doubles** (same angle), the lift…
Which of these statements correctly describes how the wing holds the aeroplane up?
options: The air on top and the air underneath must reach the end of the wing together
The wing deflects the air downwards, and the air reacts by pushing the wing up; at the same time the pressure on top is lower
The engine pulls the aeroplane up
The wing is lighter than air
questions.explanation: Newton (air deflected downwards) and Bernoulli (pressure difference) are two faces of the same phenomenon. The idea that the air must "arrive together" is a myth.

aero-02-angulo-ataque.title: Profiles and angle of attack
aero-02-angulo-ataque.theory:
# The angle of attack

The **angle of attack (α)** is the angle between the wing's **chord** (the line from the leading edge to the trailing edge) and the **relative wind** — it is not the same as the angle of the nose to the horizon.

## The lift curve

Up to near the stall, CL grows in a **straight line** with α:

```
CL = a · (α − α0)
```

- **Cambered** (curved) profiles give lift even at α = 0: their α0 is negative (here, −2°).
- A finite wing has a smaller slope than the 2D profile: `a = 2π · AR / (AR + 2)` per radian. For AR = 7.5: 4.96/rad = **0.0866 per degree**.
- Above the **critical angle** (~15°), the flow **separates** from the upper surface, CL plummets and drag shoots up: this is the **stall**.

## Altitude

At 2000 m the air has only ~82% of the sea-level density (ρ = 1.007 kg/m³). At the same speed, you need **more CL** — more angle of attack, more area or **flaps**, which increase the camber and the wing's CL.

In this slow flight (120 km/h) at 2000 m altitude, you need a lot of CL without exceeding the limit.
aero-02-angulo-ataque.task: At **120 km/h and 2000 m**, make the aeroplane fly **level** (lift between 100% and 110% of the weight) **without stalling**.
hints: Calculate the CL needed: CL = 2·W / (ρ·v²·S).
About 12.5° of angle of attack gives the right CL; above ~15° the wing stalls.
goals: Lift between 100% and 110% of the weight

questions.prompt: With CL = 0.0866·(α + 2°) and **maximum CL = 1.5**, at what angle of attack does the wing stall?
The angle of attack is the angle between…
options: the aeroplane's nose and the horizon
the wing chord and the relative wind
questions.explanation: The nose can be high and the angle of attack low (climbing) or vice versa; what matters to the wing is the relative wind.

questions.prompt: Flying higher, at the same speed, what must the pilot do to keep level flight?
options: Increase the angle of attack (the air is less dense)
questions.explanation: With lower ρ, L = ½·ρ·v²·S·CL falls; more CL (or more speed) is needed to match the weight.

aero-03-arrasto-polar.title: Drag and the drag polar
aero-03-arrasto-polar.theory:
# Two kinds of drag

The total drag of an aeroplane is the sum of:

- **Parasite drag** (`CD0`): air friction on the surface, fuselage shape, landing gear, antennas. It grows with speed.
- **Induced drag**: the "price" of generating lift. At the wing tips the air from below escapes upwards and forms **vortices**. It is greater at **low speed** (high CL).

```
CD = CD0 + CL² / (π · e · AR)
```

- `AR` = aspect ratio = span² / area. Gliders: 20–30; fighters: 2–4.
- `e` = Oswald factor (0.7–0.9): how close the lift distribution is to the ideal (elliptical).

## The polar and maximum L/D

The CL × CD graph is the **drag polar**. The line from the origin that touches the curve marks the best **L/D** (lift/drag, the aeroplane's "efficiency"):

```
(L/D)max = ½ · √(π · e · AR / CD0)      at the point where induced CD = CD0
```

With L/D = 15, the aeroplane **glides 15 m forward for every 1 m it descends**. Gliders reach 50–60!

Click ▶ Run: the angle of attack sweeps from −4° to 16° and you see the point move along the polar.
aero-03-arrasto-polar.task: Design a wing and a fuselage with a **maximum L/D of at least 15**.
hints: A higher aspect ratio reduces induced drag; a lower CD0 reduces parasite drag.
AR = 12, e = 0.85 and CD0 = 0.025 give L/D ≈ 18.

questions.prompt: A wing with AR = **8**, e = **0.8**, flying at CL = **0.5**. What is the **induced** drag coefficient?
A glider with **L/D = 15** is at a height of **1000 m**, with no wind. How many km can it glide?
Why do gliders have long, thin wings?
options: A high aspect ratio reduces induced drag and increases L/D
To fly faster than jet aircraft
questions.explanation: Induced drag is CL²/(π·e·AR): the greater the AR, the smaller it gets.

aero-04-estol.title: Stall and flaps
aero-04-estol.theory:
# The minimum speed

To fly level, L = W. Since CL has a maximum, there is a **minimum speed**, the **stall speed**:

```
Vstall = √( 2 · W / (ρ · S · CLmax) )
```

Below it no angle of attack generates enough lift: the wing exceeds the critical angle, the flow separates, the nose drops and the aeroplane loses altitude.

**Careful**: the stall happens because of **angle of attack**, not speed. In a tight turn or when pulling the stick hard, the aeroplane stalls above the level Vstall.

## How to land slower

- **Bigger wing** (lower wing loading W/S).
- **Flaps**: surfaces on the trailing edge that increase the camber and CLmax (here: +0.25 at 10°, +0.45 at 20°, +0.60 at 30°). They also increase drag — useful on landing.
- **Slats** on the leading edge (large aeroplanes) delay separation.

Pilots approach for landing at **1.3 × Vstall**, a safety margin. The "indicated" Vstall on the airspeed indicator does not change with altitude, so the simulator shows the sea-level value.

Click ▶ Run: the aeroplane decelerates until the stall.
aero-04-estol.task: Make the **stall speed 85 km/h or less** so you can land on a short runway (without changing the aeroplane's weight).
aero-04-estol.safety: Stalling close to the ground is one of the main causes of accidents in general aviation. Pilots train stall recognition and recovery with an instructor and at a safe altitude.
hints: Flaps increase CLmax: Vstall falls with the square root of CLmax.
Flaps at 30° take CLmax from 1.5 to 2.1.

questions.prompt: An aeroplane weighing **10,000 N**, wing of **15 m²**, CLmax = **1.6**, at sea level (ρ = 1.225). What is the stall speed?
What causes the stall?
options: The speed dropping below a fixed value, always
The angle of attack exceeding the critical angle, which can happen at any speed
questions.explanation: The stall is aerodynamic: the flow separates when α exceeds the critical value. In a turn or an abrupt pull-up this happens even at high speed.

questions.prompt: With Vstall = **80 km/h**, what is the recommended approach speed (1.3 × Vs)?

aero-05-decolagem.title: Take-off and climb
aero-05-decolagem.theory:
# The take-off run

On the runway, the aeroplane accelerates with:

```
m · a = Thrust − Drag − μr · (Weight − Lift)
```

- μr ≈ 0.03: rolling friction of the wheels.
- It leaves the ground at ~**1.2 × Vstall** (rotation/take-off speed).
- A quick estimate: `s ≈ V² / (2 · a_average)`.

The **propeller thrust** is `T = ηp · P / v` (power × propeller efficiency ÷ speed); at standstill it is limited (static thrust).

## Altitude and heat

At a **high** airport (or on a **hot** day) the air is less dense:

- The engine loses power (~proportional to density).
- The wing needs **more speed** for the same lift.

Result: the run gets much longer. Pilots use performance tables before every take-off.

## Climb

After leaving the ground, the **rate of climb** is the spare power divided by the weight:

```
RC = (P_available − P_required) / Weight        (m/s)
```

The certification standard measures the distance to clear a **15 m** (50 ft) obstacle.

In this problem the airport is at **2500 m** altitude and the runway is only **350 m** long.
aero-05-decolagem.task: Take off from the 350 m runway at 2500 m altitude: **leave the ground within the runway**, clear **15 m of height within 350 m** and climb at **at least 5 m/s**.
hints: Flaps reduce the take-off speed; more power gives more thrust and more climb.
Flaps at 20° and a 160 kW engine solve it.
goals: Leaves the ground within the runway
Clears 15 m of height within 350 m

questions.prompt: By the standard atmosphere (ISA), what is the air density at **2500 m**? (T = 288.15 − 0.0065·h; ρ = 1.225·(T/288.15)^4.256)
On a very hot day, the take-off run…
options: gets shorter, because hot air rises
gets longer, because hot air is less dense
questions.explanation: Hot air is less dense: the wing needs more speed and the engine produces less.

questions.prompt: An aeroplane leaves the ground at **35 m/s** with an average acceleration of **2.5 m/s²**. What is the approximate take-off run?

aero-06-estabilidade.title: Stability and control surfaces
aero-06-estabilidade.theory:
# Stable means it returns by itself

An aeroplane is **statically stable in pitch** when, if the nose is raised by a gust, a moment appears that **lowers the nose back**. What ensures this is the combination of the **centre of gravity (CG)** and the **neutral point (NP)**.

- The **neutral point** is the point where the lift increase of the whole aeroplane (wing + horizontal stabiliser) acts when the angle of attack changes.
- If the **CG is ahead of the NP**, an increase in α generates a moment that lowers the nose: **stable**.
- If the **CG is behind the NP**: the moment increases α even more — **unstable** (it only flies with a computer, like modern fighters).

```
Static margin = (h_NP − h_CG)  as a % of the mean aerodynamic chord (MAC)
```

Light aeroplanes use **5 to 20%**. A margin that is too large makes the aeroplane "heavy" and hard to raise the nose.

## The horizontal stabiliser

The wing alone has its aerodynamic centre at ~25% of the chord. The **tail** pulls the neutral point backwards. The greater the **tail volume** `VH = (S_tail · arm) / (S_wing · chord)`, the further back the NP goes (in the simulator: h_NP = 25% + 40.5% × VH).

## Control surfaces

- **Elevator** (on the horizontal stabiliser): pitch — nose up/down.
- **Ailerons** (on the wing tips, moving in opposite directions): roll.
- **Rudder** (on the vertical stabiliser): yaw — nose left/right.
aero-06-estabilidade.task: This aeroplane was loaded with the CG too far back and is **unstable**. Move the CG or enlarge the tail until the **static margin is between 5% and 20%**.
hints: The CG must be ahead of the neutral point (a smaller number in % of the chord).
With VH = 0.45 the NP is at 43%: a CG at 35% gives ~8% margin.
goals: Static margin between 5% and 20% of the MAC

questions.prompt: The neutral point is at **45%** of the MAC and the CG at **30%**. What is the static margin (in %)?
Which surface controls **roll** (banking the wings)?
questions.explanation: The ailerons go up on one side and down on the other, creating different lift on each wing.

questions.prompt: What happens if the CG is **behind** the neutral point?
options: Any pitch disturbance grows: the aeroplane is unstable
Nothing, the CG does not matter
questions.explanation: With a negative static margin the pitching moment reinforces the disturbance instead of correcting it.

aero-07-propulsao.title: Propulsion: propeller or jet?
aero-07-propulsao.theory:
# Thrust = accelerating air backwards

All aerial propulsion works by **Newton's 3rd law**: the engine throws air (or gas) backwards and the aeroplane is pushed forwards.

```
Thrust = ṁ · (Ve − V0)
```

- `ṁ` = mass flow of air (kg/s), `Ve` = speed of the exiting jet, `V0` = aeroplane speed.

## Propulsive efficiency

It is more efficient to accelerate **a lot of air a little** than **a little air a lot**:

```
η_propulsive = 2 / (1 + Ve/V0)
```

- **Propeller**: moves an enormous mass of air slowly → very efficient at low speed (up to ~600 km/h). Thrust ≈ ηp · P / v.
- **Turbojet**: fast, narrow jet → efficient only at very high speed (fighters, Concorde).
- **Turbofan**: a large fan at the front diverts most of the air **around** the core (bypass ratio 5–12 on airliners) — the middle ground that dominates airline flying.
- **Turboprop**: a turbine turning a propeller — regional aeroplanes (ATR, Embraer EMB 120).

## Consumption

- Piston/turboprop engines: specific consumption in kg of fuel per kWh (~0.2–0.3).
- Jets: TSFC in g of fuel per kN of thrust per second (~15–20 in modern turbofans).

questions.prompt: A jet engine takes in **100 kg/s** of air and expels it at **400 m/s**; the aeroplane flies at **200 m/s**. What is the thrust?
What is the propulsive efficiency of that engine (Ve = 400 m/s, V0 = 200 m/s)?
A propeller with an efficiency of **0.8** receives **100 kW** and the aeroplane flies at **50 m/s**. What is the thrust?
Why do airliners use **high-bypass** turbofans?
options: Because they accelerate a large mass of air with a small change in speed, which is more efficient
Because they are lighter than propellers
questions.explanation: η_propulsive = 2/(1 + Ve/V0): with Ve close to V0 the efficiency rises. Bypass generates thrust with "slow" air.

questions.prompt: For an agricultural aeroplane flying at 200 km/h, which propulsion makes the most sense?
questions.explanation: At low speed the propeller has the best propulsive efficiency and the lowest consumption.

aero-08-helicoptero-pairar.title: Helicopter: the rotor and hovering
aero-08-helicoptero-pairar.theory:
# The rotor is a spinning wing

Each blade of the main rotor is a wing. As it spins, it meets the air at a speed that grows from the centre to the tip (`v = Ω · r`). The pilot changes the **collective pitch** (the angle of all the blades at once) to increase or decrease the thrust.

## Momentum theory

To hover, the rotor must push air down with a force equal to the weight. The speed it gives the air (induced velocity) and the ideal power are:

```
v_i = √( T / (2 · ρ · A) )          A = π · R²
P_ideal = T · v_i = T^1.5 / √(2 · ρ · A)
```

- **Bigger rotor** (larger A) → less power for the same weight. That is why helicopters have huge rotors and cargo drones use large propellers.
- The **figure of merit** (FM ≈ 0.7) is the ratio P_ideal / P_real (profile, tip and air-rotation losses).

## Rotor limits

- **Blade stall**: each blade has a maximum CL; a rotor's thrust is limited to CT/σ ≈ 0.13 (σ = solidity = blade area / disc area). More blades, wider blades, more rpm or a bigger rotor raise the limit.
- **Tip Mach**: if the blade tip approaches the speed of sound (Mach 0.9+), shock waves, noise and loss of efficiency appear. Tips stay at ~200–220 m/s (Mach 0.6–0.65).

The simulator combines blade element theory (the thrust the collective generates) with engine power. Start with a rotor that is too small and find out what to change.
aero-08-helicoptero-pairar.task: This 1100 kg helicopter **does not leave the ground**. Adjust the rotor so that it **hovers**, **without blade stall** and with the blade tip below **Mach 0.7**.
hints: A bigger rotor and more rpm increase thrust — but watch the tip Mach.
A 5 m radius and 420 rpm solve it with the same engine.

questions.prompt: What is the **ideal** power to hover with a thrust of **10,000 N**, rotor radius **5 m**, ρ = 1.225 kg/m³?
In that same case, what is the induced velocity of the air at the rotor?
Why does a **bigger** rotor need **less** power to support the same weight?
options: Because it spins slower and therefore uses no energy
Because it pushes more air at a lower speed; the ideal power is T^1.5/√(2ρA)
It is not true: the bigger rotor uses more
questions.explanation: For the same thrust, accelerating a larger mass of air to a lower speed costs less energy — the same idea as the turbofan.

aero-09-cauda-autorrotacao.title: Torque, tail rotor and autorotation
aero-09-cauda-autorrotacao.theory:
# Action and reaction in the rotor

The engine applies a **torque** to the main rotor to spin it against the blade drag. By Newton's 3rd law, the rotor applies an equal and **opposite torque to the fuselage**: with nothing to prevent it, the helicopter would spin opposite to the rotor.

```
Torque Q = P_rotor / Ω            (Ω in rad/s)
Tail thrust = Q / arm              (arm = distance from the tail rotor to the axis)
```

- More power → more torque → more tail thrust.
- **More rpm** with the same power → less torque.
- **Longer arm** → less tail thrust (but a longer fuselage).

The pilot's pedals change the tail rotor pitch and control **yaw**. The tail rotor uses ~10% of the power.

## Other solutions

- **Coaxial** or **tandem** rotors spinning in opposite directions (Kamov, Chinook): the torques cancel.
- **Fenestron** (ducted rotor) and **NOTAR** (air jet in the tail).

## Autorotation: landing without an engine

If the engine stops, the pilot **lowers the collective**. Descending, the air passes **from bottom to top** through the rotor and keeps it spinning, like a windmill. The helicopter descends in a controlled way (~10–17 m/s vertically, less with forward speed). Close to the ground the pilot does the **flare**: pulls the collective and uses the **rotor's kinetic energy** (½·I·Ω²) to slow the descent and land softly. Heavy, large rotors store more energy.
aero-09-cauda-autorrotacao.task: This helicopter's tail rotor cannot handle the torque and the fuselage spins. Make the **heading stable** with the tail rotor needing **at most 500 N**.
aero-09-cauda-autorrotacao.safety: Tail rotors spin at thousands of rpm and are almost invisible. On the ground, never approach a helicopter with turning rotors from the rear; approach from the front, in the pilot's sight.
hints: Tail thrust = torque / arm: a longer arm reduces the thrust needed.
A 5.5 m arm and a 600 N tail solve it.
goals: The tail balances the torque (stable heading)

questions.prompt: The rotor receives **150 kW** at **400 rpm** and the tail arm is **5 m**. What tail rotor thrust is needed?
In autorotation, what keeps the rotor spinning without an engine?
options: The air passing through the rotor from bottom to top while the helicopter descends
Inertia, for just a few seconds
questions.explanation: With the collective low, the upward flow produces a force on the blades that pushes them in the direction of rotation, like a windmill.

questions.prompt: Why do helicopters with **two counter-rotating rotors** (coaxial or tandem) not need a tail rotor?
options: Because the reaction torques of the two rotors have opposite directions and cancel
questions.explanation: Each rotor pushes the fuselage to one side; spinning in opposite directions, the torques cancel out.

aero-10-projeto-breguet.title: Project: sizing an aeroplane and the Breguet range
aero-10-projeto-breguet.theory:
# How far does an aeroplane fly?

As it burns fuel, the aeroplane gets lighter. Integrating this, Louis Breguet arrived at the **range equation** (for a propeller):

```
Range = (ηp / (g · c)) · (L/D) · ln(W0 / W1)
```

- `ηp` = propeller efficiency; `c` = specific consumption (kg of fuel per joule; 0.30 kg/kWh = 8.33·10⁻⁸ kg/J).
- `L/D` = aerodynamic efficiency **at cruise speed** (not necessarily the maximum).
- `W0/W1` = take-off weight / weight without the fuel.

For a jet: `Range = (V / (g · c_T)) · (L/D) · ln(W0/W1)` — which is why jets cruise fast and high.

## The design trade-offs

- **More fuel** → greater ln(W0/W1), but the aeroplane gets **heavier**: higher stall and longer take-off.
- **Bigger wing** → lower stall, but more wetted area (more parasite drag).
- **Higher aspect ratio** → higher L/D (less induced drag), but a heavier, costlier wing (not modelled here).
- **Cruise speed and altitude**: L/D depends on the cruise CL = 2W/(ρ·V²·S). Flying higher (thin air) or slower raises CL and brings the aeroplane closer to the maximum L/D.

A conceptual design engineer does exactly this: sweeps the options and finds the point that meets **all** the requirements. Watch the range × speed graph.
aero-10-projeto-breguet.task: Customer requirements: **2000 km range**, take off from a **300 m** runway (at sea level) and **stall at 95 km/h or less** in the landing configuration.
hints: More fuel increases range but raises the stall: compensate with a bigger wing and flaps.
One solution: 220 kg of fuel, AR 11, 18 m² wing, flaps at 10°, cruise at 180 km/h and 3000 m.
goals: Takes off on the 300 m runway

questions.prompt: Breguet with ηp = **0.8**, c = **0.30 kg/kWh**, L/D = **12** and W0/W1 = **1.2**. What is the range, in km?
For maximum range, a propeller aeroplane should cruise…
options: it makes no difference, range only depends on fuel
questions.explanation: In the Breguet equation for a propeller the range is proportional to L/D; it is maximum where induced drag equals parasite drag.

questions.prompt: Does doubling an aeroplane's fuel (same aeroplane, same L/D) double its range?
options: No: the range grows with ln(W0/W1), and the extra fuel also has to be carried
Yes, and it even improves the take-off
questions.explanation: The logarithm grows more and more slowly; besides, the heavier aeroplane stalls faster and needs more runway.

aero-11-planador.title: Glider: the best glide
aero-11-planador.theory:
# Flying without an engine

A glider is always **descending** relative to the air: it trades height for speed. How far it goes for each metre it descends is the **glide ratio**, equal to the lift-to-drag ratio:

```
distance = height × (L/D)
sink rate = speed / (L/D)
```

With L/D = 25, from 2000 m you can glide **50 km** in still air. Competition gliders exceed L/D 50; an ordinary plane manages 10–15.

## The maximum L/D

From the parabolic polar CD = CD0 + CL²/(π e AR):

```
(L/D)max = ½ × √(π × e × AR / CD0)
```

Three routes: high **aspect ratio** (long, slender wings → less induced drag), high **Oswald** factor (good lift distribution, well-made tips) and low **CD0** (smooth surfaces, slim fuselage, retracted gear).

## But it must also fly slowly

Gliders climb in **thermals** — columns of warm air, sometimes only a few hundred metres across. To circle inside them, they must fly **slowly** without stalling: low **wing loading** (mass/area), which gives a low stall speed.

## In this lab

A **350 kg** glider (with pilot), 10 m² wing and CLmax 1.4. You can change the wing geometry and the area.
aero-11-planador.task: Design the glider's wing to have a **(L/D)max of at least 25** and a **stall speed of up to 70 km/h** (to circle in thermals).
hints: Aspect ratio matters most: take it near the maximum (16). Then improve Oswald and CD0.
With 10 m² the stall is at ~72 km/h. A bit more area solves it.

questions.prompt: A glider with **L/D = 25** is at **2000 m**, in still air. How far can it glide?
Flying at **90 km/h** with L/D = **30**, what is the sink rate (how many m/s does it descend)?
questions.explanation: 90 km/h = 25 m/s. 25 / 30 ≈ 0.83 m/s — any thermal stronger than that makes the glider climb.

questions.prompt: What is the (L/D)max of a wing with AR = **16**, e = **0.9** and CD0 = **0.016**?

aero-12-curvas-fator-carga.title: Turns and load factor
aero-12-curvas-fator-carga.theory:
# Bank to turn

A plane turns by **banking its wings** (bank angle φ). The lift, which was vertical, now has a horizontal part — that's what makes the turn. To keep its height, the vertical part must still equal the weight, so the total lift **increases**:

```
load factor  n = L / W = 1 / cos φ
```

At 60° of bank, n = 2: the wings hold up **twice the weight**, and the pilot feels "2 g".

## Stall speed rises in a turn

The stall speed grows with the square root of n:

```
V_stall,turn = V_stall × √n
```

A plane that stalls at 100 km/h in straight flight stalls at **~141 km/h** in a 60° turn. Tight, slow turns near the ground (as on the approach to land) are a classic cause of accidents.

## Radius and rate of turn

```
radius   r = v² / (g × tan φ)
rate     ω = g × tan φ / v
```

At 50 m/s and 30° of bank: r ≈ **441 m** and ω ≈ **6.5 °/s**. The instruments' "standard rate turn" is **3 °/s** (360° in 2 minutes).

## Structural limits

Each plane has a certified maximum load factor: ~3.8 g for normal-category planes, 6 g for aerobatic ones. Going beyond can bend or break the structure. Gusts also produce load factor: that's why there is a maximum speed for turbulent air.

questions.prompt: What is the load factor in a level turn at **60°** of bank?
A plane stalls at **100 km/h** in straight flight. At what speed does it stall in a **60°** turn?
What is the radius of a turn at **50 m/s** with **30°** of bank? (g = 9.81 m/s²)
In that turn (50 m/s, 30°), what is the rate of turn in degrees per second?
Why is a tight, slow turn near the ground dangerous?
options: Because the wind is always stronger near the ground
Because the bank raises the stall speed, and there's no height to recover
questions.explanation: With n > 1 the stall happens at a higher speed; if it comes near the ground, there's no height left to recover from the spin.

aero-13-teto.title: Rate of climb and service ceiling
aero-13-teto.theory:
# Climbing is spare power

A plane climbs when the available power exceeds the power needed for level flight. The **rate of climb** is the excess divided by the weight:

```
RC = (P_available − P_required) / W
```

With 30 kW of excess and 1100 kg: RC = 30 000 / (1100 × 9.81) ≈ **2.8 m/s**.

## Why the climb runs out

With altitude the air becomes less dense (σ = ρ/ρ0):

- A normally aspirated piston engine loses power roughly in proportion to σ. At 6000 m, σ ≈ 0.54: of 120 kW, ~65 kW remain.
- The plane has to fly **faster** for the same lift, and induced drag (which dominates in slow flight) weighs more.

At some point the excess reaches zero: that's the **absolute ceiling**. In practice one uses the **service ceiling**, where the rate of climb falls to **0.5 m/s** (100 ft/min).

## How to climb higher

- **More power** (or a turbocharger, which keeps the power up to a certain altitude).
- **High-aspect-ratio wing**: up high the flight is "slow" for the density, and induced drag rules — long wings reduce it. That's why high-altitude aircraft (U-2, wave gliders) have huge, slender wings.
- **Less weight**.

## In this lab

A 1000 kg plane + 100 kg of fuel, 16 m² wing, propeller efficiency 0.8, 120 kW normally aspirated engine. The ceiling is computed with the engine losing power with density.
aero-13-teto.task: The plane must cross a mountain range: **service ceiling of at least 8500 m** and **rate of climb of at least 8 m/s** at sea level. Adjust the **power**, the **aspect ratio**, the **mass** and the **wing area**.
hints: Power alone works, but it's expensive: with 180 kW the ceiling passes 8500 m. See how much aspect ratio helps.
With AR 10, about 150 kW is enough.
goals: Service ceiling of at least 8500 m
Rate of climb of at least 8 m/s

questions.prompt: An **1100 kg** plane has **30 kW** of spare power. What is its rate of climb? (g = 9.81 m/s²)
By the standard atmosphere, at 6000 m σ = ((288.15 − 0.0065 × 6000) / 288.15)^4.256. How much power is left of a **120 kW** normally aspirated engine (power ∝ σ)?
Why do high-aspect-ratio wings help to climb higher?
options: Because in thin air induced drag dominates, and long wings reduce it
Because they cut the stall speed to zero
questions.explanation: Up high the plane needs a high CL to stay up, and induced drag ∝ CL²/AR grows: more AR, less power required.

aero-14-curva-potencia.title: The power curve: minimum drag and minimum power
aero-14-curva-potencia.theory:
# U-shaped drag

Total drag in level flight has two parts that go in opposite directions:

- **Parasite** (friction, form): grows with v².
- **Induced** (the cost of making lift): falls with 1/v² — flying slowly requires a high CL.

The sum has a **minimum**. With the polar CD = CD0 + k CL² (k = 1/(π e AR)):

```
(L/D)max = 1 / (2 √(k × CD0))
D_min = W / (L/D)max
V_md = √(2W / (ρ S)) × (k / CD0)^(1/4)
```

At the **minimum-drag** speed V_md, parasite and induced drag are **equal**. It's the speed of **best glide** and of **maximum range** for jet aircraft (with thrust, fuel burn follows drag).

## Power is not drag

The power required is P = D × v. Since v multiplies, the minimum of power happens **slower**:

```
V_mp = V_md / 3^(1/4) ≈ 0.76 × V_md
```

At the **minimum-power** speed the plane stays aloft longest on the same fuel (**maximum endurance** for a propeller plane) and sinks slowest when gliding.

## The back side of the curve

Below V_mp, flying **slower takes more power** — counter-intuitive. On a slow approach, if the pilot pulls the nose up to "stretch" the glide, the plane slows down, needs more power and sinks more.

## Example

W = 10 000 N, S = 15 m², CD0 = 0.03, k = 0.05, ρ = 1.225: (L/D)max ≈ 12.9; D_min ≈ 775 N; V_md ≈ 37.5 m/s; P ≈ 29 kW; V_mp ≈ 28.5 m/s.

questions.prompt: What is the (L/D)max of a plane with CD0 = **0.03** and k = **0.05**?
With a weight of **10 000 N**, what is this plane's minimum drag?
With S = **15 m²** and ρ = **1.225 kg/m³**, at what speed does that minimum drag occur? (V_md = √(2W/(ρS)) × (k/CD0)^(1/4))
And the **minimum-power** speed (V_mp = V_md / 3^(1/4))?
Below the minimum-power speed ("back side of the curve"), flying slower…
questions.explanation: There, induced drag grows faster than the speed falls. Pulling the nose up on a slow approach only makes it worse.

aero-15-alcance-jato.title: Jet: range, altitude and cruise speed
aero-15-alcance-jato.theory:
# Breguet for jets

In a jet, fuel burn is proportional to **thrust** (TSFC: kg of fuel per N of thrust per second). Breguet's range equation becomes:

```
R = (V / (g × TSFC)) × (L/D) × ln(W0 / W1)
```

Note the **V multiplying**: unlike the propeller plane, the jet gains range by flying **faster**, as long as L/D doesn't drop too much. The optimum is a bit above the minimum-drag speed.

## Why jets fly high

In thin air, the same CL (and the same L/D) happens at a higher **true** speed: V ∝ 1/√ρ. At 11 000 m, ρ ≈ 0.36 kg/m³ — the plane flies ~1.8 times faster with the same drag. Since R ∝ V × L/D, range grows. Also, the jet engine becomes more efficient in cold air.

The limit is the **speed of sound**: near Mach 0.8–0.85 shock waves appear and drag soars. That's why airliners cruise at ~10–12 km, at ~850 km/h.

## Example

V = 200 m/s, TSFC = 18 g/(kN·s) = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵ kg/(N·s), L/D = 15, W0/W1 = 1.3:

R = 200 / (9.81 × 1.8 × 10⁻⁵) × 15 × ln 1.3 ≈ **4457 km**.

## In this lab

A business jet of 6000 kg empty with **3000 kg** of fuel, 30 m² wing, AR 8, TSFC 18 g/(kN·s). The range only counts if the plane can cruise (enough thrust and CL below 90% of the maximum).
aero-15-alcance-jato.task: Cruising at 500 km/h and 3000 m the jet doesn't reach 4000 km. Choose the cruise **altitude** and **speed** to exceed **6500 km** of range.
hints: Climb first: near 11 000 m the range grows a lot.
Up there, try speeds between 600 and 800 km/h and see where the range is largest.

questions.prompt: Breguet for a jet with V = **200 m/s**, TSFC = **1.8 × 10⁻⁵ kg/(N·s)**, L/D = **15** and W0/W1 = **1.3**. What is the range? (g = 9.81 m/s²)
How many hours does the jet take to fly **6000 km** at **700 km/h**?
Why does a jet gain range by flying high?
options: Because in thin air it flies faster at the same L/D, and range is proportional to V × L/D
Because there is no wind up there
questions.explanation: Same CL and same drag, but a higher true V: more kilometres for the same fuel (up to the Mach limit).

aero-16-peso-balanceamento.title: Weight and balance: the loaded CG and the tail
aero-16-peso-balanceamento.theory:
# Where is the CG after loading?

The CG changes with **passengers, baggage and fuel**. Before each flight the pilot computes the CG by the **moment** method (mass × arm, measured from a datum):

```
x_CG = Σ (m × x) / Σ m
```

A 600 kg empty plane at 2.0 m, an 80 kg pilot at 1.5 m and 100 kg of fuel at 2.2 m:

x_CG = (1200 + 120 + 220) / 780 ≈ **1.974 m**.

## As % of the mean chord (MAC)

If the MAC starts at 1.5 m and is 1.5 m long: (1.974 − 1.5) / 1.5 ≈ **31.6% MAC**.

## The neutral point and the tail

The plane is stable if the CG is **ahead of the neutral point** (lesson 6). In this model the neutral point is at 25% MAC (the wing's aerodynamic centre) plus the effect of the tail:

```
neutral point = 25% + 40.5% × VH
static margin = neutral point − CG
```

VH is the **tail volume** (stabiliser area × arm / (wing area × MAC)). A bigger or farther tail → neutral point further back → more margin.

## A good margin

- **Below ~5%**: barely stable, tiring to fly (and unstable if negative).
- **Above ~15–20%**: too stable, the elevator may lack the authority to flare for landing.

## In this lab

With today's load, the CG ended up at **40% MAC** — further aft than the original design expected. Resize the tail.
aero-16-peso-balanceamento.task: With the CG at **40% MAC**, the plane became unstable. Adjust the **tail volume** so the static margin ends up **between 5% and 15%**.
hints: Neutral point = 25 + 40.5 × VH. For a 10% margin, it must sit at 50%.
VH between ~0.50 and ~0.74 works.

questions.prompt: A **600 kg** empty plane with its CG at **2.0 m**, an **80 kg** pilot at **1.5 m** and **100 kg** of fuel at **2.2 m** from the datum. Where is the CG?
The MAC starts at **1.5 m** from the datum and is **1.5 m** long. At what percentage of the MAC is that CG?
With VH = **0.6** and the CG at **40%**, what is the static margin? (neutral point = 25% + 40.5% × VH)

aero-17-helicoptero-altitude.title: Helicopter in the mountains: hover ceiling
aero-17-helicoptero-altitude.theory:
# Thin air charges you twice

To hover, the rotor throws air downwards. By momentum theory, the ideal power is:

```
P_ideal = T^1.5 / √(2 ρ A)
```

With altitude, ρ falls and the **required** power grows with 1/√ρ: at 3000 m (σ ≈ 0.742), ~**16% more**. At the same time, the normally aspirated engine loses **available** power roughly in proportion to σ: 200 kW become ~**148 kW**. The two curves cross at the **hover ceiling**.

## The blades have a limit too

Rotor thrust is also limited by **blade stall**: the thrust coefficient per solidity CT/σ doesn't go above ~0.13. In thin air, the blades need more pitch for the same thrust and stall earlier.

```
solidity σ = (number of blades × chord) / (π × R)
```

More blades or wider blades = more blade area = more thrust before stall.

## What raises the ceiling

- **A bigger rotor** (larger A → less power per newton of thrust, as in lesson 8).
- **More power** (or turbines, which lose less with altitude).
- **More solidity** (blades) against stall.
- But the **blade tip** must not exceed ~0.65–0.7 Mach (noise, shock waves).

## Mountain rescue

Rescue helicopters operate at 3000–5000 m in the Andes and the Himalayas — and that's why they fly light, with minimum fuel, and prefer to land "running" (with forward speed) rather than hover.

## In this lab

An 1100 kg helicopter with a 4 m rotor, 2 blades, 400 rpm and a 150 kW engine.
aero-17-helicoptero-altitude.task: The helicopter will do rescues in a mountain range: **hover ceiling of at least 2500 m**, **vertical climb of at least 5 m/s** at sea level and blade tip **up to Mach 0.65**. Adjust the **engine**, the **rotor**, the **blades** and the **rpm**.
hints: With a 4 m rotor it can't even hover: the small rotor needs too much power and the blades stall. Increase the radius to 5 m.
Then use 3 blades and ~200 kW. Check the tip Mach: 400 rpm with 5 m gives ~0.62.
goals: Hover ceiling of at least 2500 m
Vertical climb of at least 5 m/s

questions.prompt: A rotor needs **100 kW** (ideal) to hover at sea level. How much does it need at 3000 m, where σ = ρ/ρ0 = **0.742**? (P ∝ 1/√ρ)
And how much is left at 3000 m of a **200 kW** normally aspirated engine (available power ∝ σ)?
What is the solidity of a **3-blade** rotor with a **0.25 m** chord and a **2.5 m** radius? (σ = b × c / (π R))

aero-18-rotor-avanco.title: The rotor in forward flight: the advancing and the retreating blade
aero-18-rotor-avanco.theory:
# Two blades, two speeds

In a hover, every blade sees the same wind: Ω × R at the tip. Flying forward at speed V:

- The **advancing blade** sees Ω R **+** V.
- The **retreating blade** sees Ω R **−** V.

With the tip at 220 m/s and V = 70 m/s (252 km/h), the advancing tip reaches **290 m/s (Mach 0.85)** and the retreating one drops to **150 m/s**.

## Dissymmetry of lift

If the blades had a fixed pitch, the advancing side would lift much more and the helicopter would **roll over**. The solution, by Juan de la Cierva (autogyro, 1920s), is the **flapping hinge**: the advancing blade rises (flaps up), which lowers its effective angle of attack; the retreating one drops and gains angle. The **cyclic swashplate** also adjusts each blade's pitch around the revolution.

## Advance ratio

```
μ = V / (Ω R)
```

With μ ≈ 0.3, the helicopter is already near its limit.

## Speed limits

- **Retreating-blade stall**: to make up for its low speed, it needs a lot of pitch — and stalls. Strong vibration, roll towards the retreating side.
- **Compressibility on the advancing blade**: near Mach 0.9 shock waves, noise and drag appear.
- At the root of the retreating blade there is even a region of **reverse flow**.

That's why conventional helicopters stay below ~300 km/h. To go further: **rigid coaxial rotors with a pusher propeller** (X3, SB-1), or the **tilt-rotor** (V-22), which becomes an aeroplane in cruise.

## Solidity

σ = b c / (π R): 4 blades of 0.5 m on a 7 m rotor give σ ≈ 0.091.

questions.prompt: The blade tip spins at **220 m/s** and the helicopter flies at **70 m/s**. What is the advancing tip's Mach number? (sound at 340 m/s)
And the airspeed at the tip of the **retreating** blade?
What is the advance ratio μ = V / (ΩR) in that flight?
What is the solidity of a **4-blade** rotor with a **0.5 m** chord and a **7 m** radius?
What limits the top speed of a conventional helicopter?
options: The weight of the tail rotor
Retreating-blade stall and compressibility on the advancing blade
Always a lack of engine power
questions.explanation: Too fast, the retreating blade needs too much pitch and stalls, while the advancing tip nears the speed of sound.

aero-19-autorrotacao.title: Autorotation: designing a rotor that saves lives
aero-19-autorrotacao.theory:
# Without an engine, the rotor becomes a parachute

If the engine quits, the pilot **lowers the collective**: the air coming up through the disc keeps the rotor turning (lesson 9), and the rotor brakes the descent like a parachute. The descent rate settles at:

```
v_descent ≈ √(2 W / (ρ × A × 1.2))
```

A 1600 kg helicopter with a 5.6 m rotor comes down at ~**14.7 m/s** (almost 53 km/h): too fast to touch the ground.

## The flare

Near the ground, the pilot **raises the collective**: the blades gain pitch and use the **rotational energy** stored in the rotor to brake the descent. The available energy is:

```
E = ½ × I × Ω² × (1 − 0.7²)
```

(the rotor can lose up to ~30% of its rpm before the blades stall; with I = 8 × blades × chord × R³ in this model). If this energy exceeds the descent's kinetic energy (½ m v²), the touchdown is soft.

## What makes a good autorotation rotor

- **A large rotor**: descends more slowly (larger A) **and** stores much more energy (I ∝ R³).
- **Heavy/wide blades** and more blades: more inertia.
- **High rpm**: energy ∝ Ω², but the **tip** must not exceed ~Mach 0.65.

There's a trade-off: high inertia makes the rotor slow to spin up and respond; light rotors are agile but lose rpm quickly after a failure.

## In this lab

A **1600 kg** helicopter, 4.5 m rotor, 2 blades of 0.25 m at 450 rpm. It comes down too fast and has no energy for the flare.
aero-19-autorrotacao.task: Redesign the rotor so an engine failure ends in a **safe landing** (touchdown at up to 3 m/s), with an **autorotation descent of up to 15 m/s** and blade tip **up to Mach 0.65**.
aero-19-autorrotacao.safety:
- Practice autorotations are done **with an instructor**, at a safe height and over a prepared landing area; most end with a "power recovery" before touchdown.
- Know the model's **height–velocity diagram** ("dead man's curve"): some combinations of low height and low speed don't allow a safe landing after an engine failure.
hints: To come down at 15 m/s with 1600 kg the rotor needs ~95 m² of disc: a radius of ~5.5 m.
With a bigger radius, lower the rpm so the tip stays under Mach 0.65 (5.6 m at ~370 rpm).
goals: Safe landing (touchdown at up to 3 m/s)
Autorotation descent of up to 15 m/s

questions.prompt: What is the autorotation descent rate of a **1600 kg** helicopter with a **5.6 m** rotor radius? (v = √(2W/(ρ A 1.2)), ρ = 1.225, g = 9.81)
That rotor has 2 blades with a **0.25 m** chord and spins at **370 rpm**. What is its rotational energy ½ I Ω², with I = 8 × blades × chord × R³?
If the rotor can lose up to **30%** of its rpm during the flare, what percentage of its rotational energy can be used?
questions.explanation: Energy goes with Ω²: 0.7² = 49% remains. 1 − 0.49 = 51% can be used.

aero-20-projeto-mato.title: Final project: a short-field plane for remote regions
aero-20-projeto-mato.theory:
# The plane that connects places with no road

**Short-field** planes ("bush planes") carry doctors, vaccines and cargo to isolated places — in the Amazon, the Andes, Alaska. The requirements pull in opposite directions:

- **Take off short and at altitude** (lessons 4, 5): low **wing loading**, **flaps**, power.
- **Go far** (lesson 10): high **L/D** — a high-aspect-ratio wing —, enough fuel and an efficient cruise.
- **Climb well** after takeoff to clear hills (lesson 13).
- **Land slowly** and safely: low stall speed.

## Wing loading

```
wing loading = mass / wing area
```

A 920 kg plane with a 16 m² wing has 57.5 kg/m². The stall speed comes from V = √(2W / (ρ S CLmax)); with 20° flaps (CLmax 1.5 + 0.45 = 1.95): **~78 km/h**.

## The trade-offs

- A **bigger** wing lowers the stall and the ground roll, but adds wetted area and lowers the cruise L/D.
- **Full** flaps (30°) give the highest CL, but also lots of drag: on takeoff, acceleration drops. 10–20° is usually best for takeoff; 30° for landing.
- **More fuel** increases range, but weighs: higher stall, longer roll.

## In this lab

A 700 kg empty plane, **130 kW** engine (fixed), CLmax 1.5, a **300 m** runway at **1500 m** altitude, cruise at 200 km/h and 2000 m.
aero-20-projeto-mato.task: Close the design: take off and clear 15 m **within 220 m** on the runway at 1500 m, **stall at up to 80 km/h**, **range of at least 2200 km** and **climb of at least 7 m/s**. Choose the **wing area and aspect ratio**, the **takeoff flaps** and the **fuel**.
hints: Start with the stall: with 14 m² and no flaps it's above 90 km/h. About 16 m² and 20° of flaps fix the stall and the takeoff.
For range, raise the aspect ratio (~9) and carry ~220 kg of fuel. Check the stall stays below 80 km/h.

questions.prompt: What is the wing loading of a **920 kg** plane with a **16 m²** wing?
With a CLmax of **1.95** (20° flaps), what is this plane's stall speed (920 kg, 16 m², ρ = 1.225, g = 9.81)?
Why are 20° flaps usually better than the full 30° for takeoff?
options: Because 30° adds a lot of drag and the plane accelerates and climbs worse
Because flaps only work for landing
questions.explanation: The last stage of flap adds little extra CL and a lot of drag: great for slowing down on landing, bad for accelerating and climbing.
